questions.question: At what object size does the .NET GC place an allocation on the Large Object Heap (LOH) instead of the normal small-object heap?

choices.text: 85,000 bytes
8,000 bytes
1 MB, matching the default gen 2 segment size
There's no fixed threshold; it depends on available memory

questions.explanation: An object >= 85,000 bytes is allocated on the LOH; this threshold was determined by performance tuning and is a fixed constant, not memory-dependent. 8,000 bytes and 1 MB are plausible-sounding but wrong numbers; 'depends on memory' misdescribes it as dynamic when it's a fixed threshold.

questions.question: Why is boxing a value type considered expensive?

choices.text: It requires a network round trip to the CLR type registry
It allocates a new object on the managed heap and adds GC pressure
It permanently locks the value type's memory for the process lifetime
It converts the value to a string internally before storing it

questions.explanation: Boxing allocates a heap object and copies the value into it, adding GC pressure and defeating the point of using a value type. There's no network call, no permanent lock, and no implicit string conversion involved.

questions.question: When an `await` is reached and the awaited task is already completed, what happens?

choices.text: The state machine always allocates on the heap and schedules a continuation
The method restarts execution from the beginning
Execution continues synchronously inline, with no thread yield
The thread pool spins up a new thread to finish the method

questions.explanation: If the awaiter's IsCompleted is already true, MoveNext() just continues executing inline — no continuation registration, no thread yield, and (if the whole method completes this way) potentially no heap allocation at all for the state machine. It doesn't restart the method or spin up a new thread.

questions.question: What effect does `ConfigureAwait(false)` have inside an ASP.NET Core request-handling method?

choices.text: It eliminates thread-pool starvation risk under any load
It forces the continuation back onto the original request thread
It suppresses exception propagation from the awaited task
ASP.NET Core has no SynchronizationContext, so it's a no-op here

questions.explanation: ASP.NET Core doesn't install a SynchronizationContext (unlike classic ASP.NET), so continuations already run on arbitrary thread pool threads regardless of ConfigureAwait — it's harmless but provides no benefit there. It doesn't prevent starvation on its own, doesn't force a specific thread, and doesn't touch exception propagation.

questions.question: Why can't a `try/catch` around the call site of a fire-and-forget `async void` method reliably catch its exceptions?

choices.text: It's rethrown on the active thread/context instead of the Task
async void methods aren't permitted to throw exceptions
The CLR automatically swallows exceptions thrown from async void
try/catch can't wrap any method containing an await expression

questions.explanation: There's no Task for async void, so its exceptions can't be stored/observed like a normal async Task method's — they're thrown directly wherever the continuation resumes, bypassing a try/catch at the call site (often crashing the process). They aren't disallowed, aren't silently swallowed, and try/catch works fine around awaited async Task methods.

questions.question: What two conditions together cause the classic async/await deadlock when calling `.Result` or `.Wait()`?

choices.text: Using ValueTask instead of Task causes the deadlock
Running the application in a Debug build configuration
Calling an async method from within a static constructor
A single-threaded context and a synchronous block

questions.explanation: The deadlock needs a context (UI thread, classic ASP.NET request thread) that the continuation is captured to and blocked on — the blocked thread can never run the continuation, so the awaited task never completes. ValueTask, Debug builds, and static constructors aren't the cause.

questions.question: Which GC mode is the ASP.NET Core default, and why?

choices.text: Workstation GC, because it minimizes memory footprint for containers
Only concurrent GC is used, with generational collection disabled entirely
Server GC, since spare cores favor parallel throughput-oriented collection
There is no default GC mode; it must always be explicitly configured

questions.explanation: Server GC runs a dedicated heap and GC thread per logical core in parallel, trading memory for throughput — the right trade-off for a typical server with spare cores, which is why it's the ASP.NET Core default. Workstation GC is the better fit for memory-constrained, low-CPU scenarios (e.g., many 1-core containers), not the ASP.NET Core default; the runtime does have a default even if unconfigured.

questions.question: What is unsafe about awaiting the same `ValueTask` (or `ValueTask<T>`) more than once?

choices.text: The pooled backing source resets, making a second await unsafe
Nothing — ValueTask can be awaited multiple times just like Task
The compiler rejects a second await with a compile-time error
It always deadlocks the thread that awaits it a second time

questions.explanation: Unlike Task (a plain object safe to observe multiple times), a ValueTask may back onto a pooled IValueTaskSource that gets reset once consumed — awaiting it again can throw, return stale data, or corrupt an unrelated operation reusing the same pooled object. It's not compile-time checked and doesn't inherently deadlock.

questions.question: You inject a Scoped service directly into a Singleton in ASP.NET Core's DI container. What's the correct description of the risk and the built-in safety net?

choices.text: The container always throws at startup, in every environment — this can never ship
It works correctly and is the recommended way to consume scoped services from singletons
The container silently creates a fresh scope automatically for each call
It becomes a captive dependency; validation only throws by default in Development

questions.explanation: This is a captive dependency: the singleton holds the scoped instance for its entire lifetime instead of getting a fresh one per request. Microsoft's docs note that scope-validation throwing this error by default only happens in the Development environment (not always, and not in every environment) — so it can slip through unnoticed in other environments. It's not automatically safe, and DI does not auto-create a new scope per call for you.

questions.question: What's the standard EF Core fix for the N+1 query problem caused by lazily-loaded navigation properties accessed in a loop?

choices.text: Wrap the loop in a single database transaction
Disable the database's query result cache
Use eager loading via .Include()/.ThenInclude() for one JOIN query
Switch the DbContext lifetime from Scoped to Singleton
Increase the database connection pool size limit

questions.explanation: .Include()/.ThenInclude() (or explicit .Load() calls) fetch related data as part of the initial query via a JOIN, turning N+1 round trips into one (or a controlled few). A transaction, connection pool size, and query caching don't address the root cause of issuing one query per entity; making DbContext a Singleton is actively wrong and unsafe (DbContext is not thread-safe and is meant to be Scoped).

questions.question: What classic design pattern does the ASP.NET Core middleware pipeline implement?

choices.text: Chain of Responsibility pattern
Observer pattern
Singleton pattern
Factory pattern

questions.explanation: Each middleware component decides independently whether to handle the request, pass it to the next one, or short-circuit — exactly Chain of Responsibility. Observer is about broadcasting events to subscribers, Singleton is about instance uniqueness, and Factory is about object creation — none describe a chain of handlers passing a request along.

questions.question: Which built-in DI lifetime creates exactly one instance per HTTP request?

choices.text: Transient
Scoped
Singleton
Static

questions.explanation: Scoped services are created once per request/scope and shared within it. Transient creates a new instance every resolution, Singleton creates one for the whole app's lifetime, and "Static" isn't a DI lifetime at all.

questions.question: Which pipeline-building method registers middleware that never calls a `next` delegate and always terminates the pipeline?

choices.text: Use
Map
Run
MapWhen

questions.explanation: `Run` registers terminal middleware with no `next` parameter — it's meant to be the last delegate in the pipeline. `Use` can continue or short-circuit, while `Map`/`MapWhen` branch the pipeline by path/predicate rather than terminating it.

questions.question: Why must `UseRouting` be registered before authorization middleware?

choices.text: Authorization needs the request body to already be parsed
UseRouting registers the DI container needed by authorization
It's purely a historical convention with no functional reason
Authorization needs the endpoint routing selects to check its metadata

questions.explanation: `UseRouting` matches the request to an endpoint and stores it on `HttpContext` without running it; authorization needs that selected endpoint to read its `[Authorize]` metadata, so it must run afterward. Body parsing and DI container setup are unrelated to routing/auth ordering, and it's a functional requirement, not just convention.

questions.question: Which options interface is itself registered as a singleton, can be injected into other singletons, and always reflects the latest configuration?

choices.text: IOptionsMonitor<T>
IOptions<T>
IOptionsSnapshot<T>
IConfiguration

questions.explanation: `IOptionsMonitor<T>` is a singleton with an always-current `CurrentValue` and change notifications via `OnChange`. `IOptions<T>` is frozen at startup, `IOptionsSnapshot<T>` is scoped (so it can't go into a singleton), and `IConfiguration` is the raw, untyped configuration source rather than a bound options object.

questions.question: What is a "captive dependency" in ASP.NET Core's DI container?

choices.text: A circular reference between two singleton services
A scoped/transient service kept alive for the app's life by a singleton
A service that fails to resolve because its dependencies aren't registered
A middleware that captures and logs every incoming request

questions.explanation: A singleton that takes a scoped (or transient) service as a constructor dependency resolves it once and holds that instance forever, defeating the shorter-lived service's intended scoping. The other options describe unrelated problems: circular references, missing registrations, and request logging.

questions.question: By default, what happens if code resolves a scoped service directly from the root `IServiceProvider` in Production?

choices.text: Yes, it always throws regardless of environment
No, but it logs a warning to the console
Yes, but only if ValidateOnBuild is enabled
No — Production disables scope validation by default, so it fails silently

questions.explanation: `ValidateScopes` defaults to on in Development (where it throws immediately) and off in Production, so the scoped service is silently created once from the root container and effectively promoted to singleton behavior — no exception, no warning, just a latent shared-state bug.

questions.question: `IHttpContextAccessor` is registered as a singleton. How does it still return the context for the currently executing request?

choices.text: It relies on AsyncLocal<T> to flow the request's context through async calls
It creates a new instance per request internally
ASP.NET Core restarts the singleton on every request
It reads the context from a static dictionary keyed by thread ID

questions.explanation: The accessor itself stays a single singleton instance, but its `HttpContext` property reads ambient state flowed via `AsyncLocal<T>` through the current request's async call chain. It isn't re-instantiated per request, the runtime doesn't restart singletons, and it isn't thread-ID-keyed (which would break under async continuations that hop threads).

questions.question: What problem do "keyed services" (introduced in .NET 8) solve?

choices.text: They allow a service to have multiple constructors
They enable property injection in the built-in container
Registering/resolving multiple implementations of an interface by a key
They replace the need for interfaces entirely

questions.explanation: Keyed services let you register several implementations of the same interface under distinct keys and resolve a specific one via `[FromKeyedServices(key)]`, replacing older workarounds like filtering an injected `IEnumerable<T>`. They don't affect constructor overloading, add property injection, or remove the need for interfaces.

questions.question: What's a real factor favoring MVC controllers over minimal APIs for a large, long-lived API surface?

choices.text: Controllers run measurably faster under all workloads
Built-in conventions (binding, filters) that scale better for large teams
Controllers can use dependency injection while minimal APIs cannot
Minimal APIs cannot use middleware at all

questions.explanation: Controllers bring conventions like model binding and the action filter pipeline that help large teams keep many endpoints consistent. Minimal APIs actually have somewhat lower per-request overhead (not higher), fully support DI, and run on the same middleware pipeline as controllers.

questions.question: By default, how does EF Core's change tracker detect that a property on a tracked entity has changed?

choices.text: It requires entities to implement INotifyPropertyChanged
It diffs current values against a stored per-property snapshot
It re-queries the database before every SaveChanges call
It relies on the CLR's garbage collector to flag mutated objects

questions.explanation: EF Core's default strategy is snapshot-based: it stores each property's value when the entity starts being tracked, then diffs against that snapshot during DetectChanges (called internally by SaveChanges). (a) describes change-tracking proxies, an opt-in alternative, not the default. (c) would defeat the purpose of tracking changes made only in memory. (d) isn't a real mechanism EF Core uses.

questions.question: A tracking query returns an entity that's already present in the change tracker. What does EF Core do?

choices.text: Throws a duplicate-key tracking exception immediately
Creates and tracks a brand-new instance alongside the old one
Returns the already-tracked instance instead of a new one
Automatically detaches the older instance from the context

questions.explanation: Tracking queries do identity resolution: if the entity is already tracked, EF Core hands back that same instance rather than creating a duplicate, which can use less memory and be faster than a no-tracking query for that case. (a), (b), and (d) don't match documented behavior.

questions.question: Including two sibling collection navigations on the same entity in one query (e.g. Blog.Posts and Blog.Contributors) can cause which specific problem?

choices.text: A cartesian explosion from the cross product of the two collections' rows
A compile-time error, since EF Core disallows multiple collection includes
Silent data loss for one of the two navigations
An automatic fallback to lazy loading for both navigations

questions.explanation: Joining two collection navigations at the same level produces a cross product per parent row, multiplying result rows unnecessarily. (b) is false, this compiles and runs fine, it's just slow. (c) and (d) don't reflect what actually happens.

questions.question: What's the main downside of AsSplitQuery() compared to the default single-query behavior?

choices.text: It cannot be combined with the Include() method at all
It disables change tracking for every entity in the result
No single-snapshot guarantee, since each round trip is separate
It only works with the SQL Server provider and no others

questions.explanation: Because split queries are separate round trips, most databases give no atomic-snapshot guarantee across them, so concurrent writes between the queries can produce inconsistent results. (a) is false, split queries are specifically for Include scenarios. (b) is unrelated, tracking is independent of single vs. split. (d) is false, it's a general relational-provider feature.

questions.question: For lazy-loading proxies to work on a navigation property, what must be true of that property and its containing class?

choices.text: Must be virtual on a class that isn't sealed
The property must be static and marked with [Lazy]
The class must implement IEnumerable directly
The property must return a Task-wrapped type

questions.explanation: Proxy-based lazy loading generates a runtime subclass that overrides navigation properties, which requires them to be virtual on a class that can be inherited from (not sealed). (b), (c), and (d) don't describe any real EF Core requirement.

questions.question: Why do two queries with the same shape but different inline literal constants (e.g. `p.Title == "post1"` vs `p.Title == "post2"`) get compiled and cached separately by EF Core?

choices.text: Because the literal becomes part of the expression tree, changing its shape
Because string comparisons are never cached by EF Core under any circumstance
Because the query cache only holds one entry per DbContext type
Because literals force EF Core into client-side evaluation

questions.explanation: EF Core caches compiled queries by expression-tree shape; a captured variable becomes a parameter (same shape regardless of value), but an inline constant is baked into the tree, so each distinct literal produces a distinct shape and a separate cache entry. (b), (c), and (d) misstate how the cache actually works.

questions.question: How do ExecuteUpdate() and ExecuteDelete() differ from the traditional query-then-SaveChanges() approach for bulk changes?

choices.text: They queue changes in the change tracker for the next SaveChanges call
They issue one SQL statement immediately, bypassing the change tracker
They require every affected row to be loaded into memory first, like SaveChanges does
They only work when wrapped in an explicit transaction

questions.explanation: ExecuteUpdate/ExecuteDelete skip querying and tracking entirely and issue one direct SQL UPDATE/DELETE immediately. (a) describes SaveChanges' actual model, the opposite of these methods. (c) is exactly what they avoid. (d) is false, they don't require a transaction, though multiple calls aren't atomic together without one.

questions.question: A Post entity has a required navigation to Blog, and Blog has a global query filter. What can happen when you run `context.Posts.Include(p => p.Blog)`?

choices.text: The required navigation's INNER JOIN drops posts whose Blog was filtered out
EF Core throws a compile-time error for combining filters with required navigations
The query filter on Blog is automatically ignored whenever Include is used
Posts are returned with a null Blog reference instead of being filtered

questions.explanation: Required navigations translate to INNER JOINs, so if the related Blog row was excluded by its query filter, the Post row has no join partner and is silently dropped from the result too. (b) is false, it's a runtime data issue, not a compile error. (c) and (d) don't match documented behavior.

questions.question: Where in a LINQ query does EF Core (since 3.0) permit implicit client-side evaluation without throwing?

choices.text: Only inside the top-level projection (the final Select)
Anywhere in the query, matching pre-3.0 behavior
Only inside OrderBy clauses
Nowhere; all client evaluation requires an explicit opt-in

questions.explanation: Since EF Core 3.0, client evaluation is allowed only in the top-level projection; a non-translatable call anywhere else (like inside Where) throws a runtime exception instead of silently evaluating client-side. (b) describes the old, pre-3.0 behavior. (c) isn't accurate. (d) is too strict, the projection case is allowed implicitly.

questions.question: Which of the following are documented reasons EF Core throws an InvalidOperationException for concurrent DbContext use? (select all that apply)

choices.text: An async call wasn't awaited before the context was used again
The same context instance was used concurrently from multiple threads
A LINQ query used a lambda expression instead of a method group
The context was registered with a transient lifetime in DI

questions.explanation: Both a missing await on an async EF Core call and genuine multi-threaded sharing of one context instance are documented causes of the concurrent-access exception. (c) is unrelated to concurrency, it's a syntax choice with no runtime effect here. (d) is a DI lifetime choice, not itself a cause of concurrent access.

questions.question: At what object size does the CLR allocate on the Large Object Heap instead of the normal small-object heap?

choices.text: 1,024 bytes
16,384 bytes
85,000 bytes

questions.explanation: Objects at or above 85,000 bytes go on the Large Object Heap (LOH), which is collected only during generation 2 GCs. 1,024 and 16,384 bytes are plausible-sounding round numbers but aren't the actual threshold; 1,048,576 bytes (1 MB) is far too large and would make most large arrays never qualify.

questions.question: Why must `Span<T>` be declared as a `ref struct`?

choices.text: To make it faster to pass as a method parameter
So the compiler can enforce a stack-only lifetime for it
To force the JIT to inline every method that uses it
To allow it to implement multiple interfaces without boxing

questions.explanation: Span<T> can wrap stack memory (e.g. from stackalloc), so it must never escape to the heap where that pointer could become invalid; ref struct is the compiler mechanism enforcing stack-only usage. It's not primarily about parameter-passing speed, inlining, or interface implementation — those are side effects, not the reason.

questions.question: Which GC flavor does ASP.NET Core use by default?

choices.text: Workstation GC, non-concurrent
Workstation GC, background
Server GC, non-concurrent
Server GC, background

questions.explanation: ASP.NET Core defaults to Server GC running in background (concurrent) mode, since the host determines the default GC flavor for hosted apps and a web server is the high-throughput scenario Server GC targets. The Workstation options are the standalone-app default, not the hosted-app default.

questions.question: What does `ArrayPool<T>.Rent(minimumLength)` guarantee about the array it returns?

choices.text: At least minimumLength; contents aren't guaranteed cleared
An array of exactly minimumLength, zero-filled
An array of exactly minimumLength, contents not guaranteed cleared
An array of at least minimumLength, always zero-filled

questions.explanation: Rent retrieves a buffer that is at least the requested length — it may be larger — and by default Return doesn't clear the array's contents for performance, so the caller must track and use only the logical length it requested. The exact-length options are wrong because pooled arrays are commonly reused and thus larger than requested; the always-zero-filled option is wrong because clearing is opt-in via Return's clearArray parameter.

questions.question: An object overrides Finalize(). What happens the first time a GC discovers it's otherwise unreachable?

choices.text: Its memory is reclaimed immediately, then Finalize runs afterward
It's promoted to generation 2 permanently and never finalized
The GC throws an exception because Finalize wasn't suppressed
It's queued for finalization, kept alive until finalized

questions.explanation: The object is moved off the finalization queue onto a queue of objects ready to be finalized, kept alive so a finalizer thread can run Finalize, and only becomes eligible for actual reclamation on a subsequent collection — this is why finalizable objects need at least two GCs. Reclaiming memory before finalizing would let a finalizer touch freed memory; permanent Gen2 promotion and an exception aren't part of the documented mechanism.

questions.question: In `dotnet-counters`, which combination most directly confirms a GC-pressure problem rather than a purely CPU-bound one?

choices.text: High CPU usage with a normal allocation rate and low % Time in GC
Low allocation rate with high thread pool queue length
High allocation rate with elevated % Time in GC
High working set with zero exceptions thrown

questions.explanation: A high allocation rate driving frequent generational collections and a meaningfully elevated % Time in GC is the direct signature of GC pressure. High CPU with normal allocation and low % Time in GC points to CPU-bound work unrelated to GC; thread pool queue length points to concurrency/async saturation; working set with no exceptions says little about GC specifically.

questions.question: In BenchmarkDotNet's MemoryDiagnoser output, what does the "Gen 0" column actually represent?

choices.text: The percentage of total runtime spent in Gen0 collections
The number of Gen0 collections per 1,000 operations of the benchmarked method
The size in bytes of the Gen0 segment at the end of the benchmark
The exact number of Gen0 collections observed during the entire run

questions.explanation: BenchmarkDotNet's own documentation defines the Gen X columns as collections per 1,000 operations, normalizing across benchmarks with different iteration counts — not a raw total count, a time percentage, or a segment size, all of which are plausible-sounding but incorrect readings of the column.

questions.question: What is the key difference between GCLatencyMode.LowLatency and GCLatencyMode.SustainedLowLatency?

choices.text: SustainedLowLatency disables generation 0 collections entirely
They're functionally identical, just named differently across .NET versions
LowLatency isn't for Server GC; SustainedLowLatency fits a longer duration
LowLatency works under Server GC; SustainedLowLatency doesn't

questions.explanation: LowLatency is documented as not available for the server garbage collector and is meant for short bounded critical sections, while SustainedLowLatency is designed to minimize latency over an extended period by avoiding full blocking collections. They are not identical, and neither mode disables Gen0 collections — SustainedLowLatency still allows Gen0/Gen1/concurrent Gen2 collections.

questions.question: Does a Native AOT-published .NET app use a different garbage collector than a normal JIT-based app?

choices.text: Yes — Native AOT replaces the GC with a simpler reference-counting collector
No — it ships a stripped-down CoreCLR that still uses the same generational GC
Yes — Native AOT uses a mark-and-sweep collector without generations
No — Native AOT apps disable garbage collection entirely and require manual memory management

questions.explanation: Native AOT changes the compilation/execution model (no JIT, ahead-of-time compiled) and bundles a stripped-down CoreCLR runtime, but that runtime still provides the same generational GC. It doesn't replace the collector with reference counting or plain mark-and-sweep, and it doesn't disable garbage collection or require manual memory management.

questions.question: Which of the following operations can silently box a struct? (Select all that apply.)

choices.text: Adding the struct to a non-generic ArrayList
Passing the struct to a method parameter typed as object
Storing the struct in a List<T> of its own concrete type
Calling an interface method on the struct through the interface type

questions.explanation: ArrayList stores object internally so any struct added is boxed; an object-typed parameter requires boxing to accept a value type; calling an interface method via the interface type on a struct typically boxes it too. A List<T> of the struct's own concrete type stores the value type directly and contiguously without boxing, which is exactly why generics were introduced.

questions.question: Two `record class` instances have identical property values but were constructed as separate objects. What does `record1 == record2` evaluate to?

choices.text: True — records compare every property's value, not identity
False — records use reference equality like plain classes
Throws unless GetHashCode is manually overridden first
True only when both instances are boxed to object first

questions.explanation: The `record` modifier generates value equality: `Equals`/`GetHashCode`/`==`/`!=` all compare every property's value. Two records with identical property values are equal even though they're distinct objects (ReferenceEquals is false). (b) describes plain classes, not records. (c) is wrong — no override is required, the compiler generates it. (d) boxing has no bearing on record equality.

questions.question: For a `record struct`, does a `with` expression allocate a new object on the heap the way it does for a `record class`?

choices.text: No — it's just another value copy, no heap allocation needed
Yes, both use the same compiler-generated Clone method
No, record structs never support with expressions
Yes, but only if the struct implements IEquatable

questions.explanation: record struct is a value type, so assignment (and `with`) already copies the whole value — no heap allocation or clone method involved. record class needs a heap allocation because `with` copies via a compiler-generated clone method on the reference type. (b) is wrong — record structs don't use a Clone method. (c) is factually wrong, record structs do support `with`. (d) IEquatable is unrelated to with-expression mechanics.

questions.question: What C# language construct is the compiler mechanism that makes LINQ's deferred execution possible?

choices.text: Reflection over the IEnumerable interface at runtime
The `dynamic` keyword deferring type resolution
The `yield return` statement inside an iterator block
The `async`/`await` keywords compiling to a state machine

questions.explanation: Deferred execution is supported directly by `yield return` inside an iterator block, which the compiler turns into a state machine implementing IEnumerator<T>. (a) reflection plays no role here. (b) `dynamic` is unrelated — it defers type checking, not sequence evaluation. (d) async/await is a different, unrelated state-machine mechanism for asynchronous continuation, not lazy sequence iteration.

questions.question: A method has `IEnumerable<int> query = source.Where(...)`. The caller calls `query.Count()` then `query.ToList()`. What happens?

choices.text: ToList() throws because the query was already consumed
Count() and ToList() run in parallel automatically
The Where filter runs once, results are cached after Count()
The Where filter runs twice — once per enumeration

questions.explanation: A deferred query variable stores no results — each terminal call (Count(), ToList()) re-enumerates the whole chain from scratch. (a) is wrong, IEnumerable queries aren't 'consumed' and can be enumerated repeatedly. (b) there's no automatic parallelism in LINQ to Objects. (c) is the common wrong assumption — nothing caches results unless you explicitly materialize with ToList()/ToArray().

questions.question: What's the key structural difference between how `Where` behaves on an `IEnumerable<T>` versus an `IQueryable<T>`?

choices.text: IQueryable's Where always executes on a background thread
IEnumerable uses a delegate, IQueryable an expression tree
There is no difference — both compile to identical IL
IQueryable's Where requires the source to implement ICollection

questions.explanation: IEnumerable<T>'s Where takes a Func<T,bool> — a compiled, in-process delegate. IQueryable<T>'s Where takes an Expression<Func<T,bool>> — an inspectable expression tree a provider (e.g. EF Core) can translate to SQL. (a) no threading guarantee exists. (c) they compile to genuinely different overloads with different behavior. (d) ICollection isn't required by either interface's Where.

questions.question: Since EF Core 3.0, what happens by default if part of a `Where` clause can't be translated to SQL?

choices.text: EF Core silently ignores that part of the filter
The query falls back to raw SQL execution
EF Core throws instead of evaluating it client-side
EF Core automatically rewrites the query into a translatable form

questions.explanation: EF Core 3.x changed the default so untranslatable filtering logic throws at runtime instead of silently falling back to client evaluation (pulling extra data to finish filtering in memory) — this prevents a query that quietly does far more work than intended from shipping unnoticed. (a) and (d) don't reflect actual behavior. (b) there's no raw-SQL fallback mechanism triggered this way.

questions.question: Why is `if (obj is int number)` generally preferred over `if (obj is int) { int number = (int)obj; }`?

choices.text: It's identical in every way, just shorter to type
It avoids one unboxing operation compared to the cast form
It compiles to a hidden try/catch around the cast
It's null-safe and never risks InvalidCastException

questions.explanation: The declaration/type pattern safely tests and binds in one step — no cast that could throw InvalidCastException, and it correctly rejects null regardless of compile-time type, unlike an explicit cast which can throw. (a) undersells real behavioral differences. (b) the number of unboxing operations isn't the actual reason it's preferred. (c) there's no try/catch involved — it's a type test, not exception handling.

questions.question: With `<Nullable>enable</Nullable>` turned on, what changes about the compiled program's runtime behavior for a `string?` versus a `string`?

choices.text: Nothing — both compile to System.String at runtime
string? is compiled as Nullable<string> under the hood
string? adds a runtime null-check before every dereference
string becomes a non-nullable value type at runtime

questions.explanation: Nullable reference types are entirely a compile-time, static-analysis feature — the runtime behavior of the program is unchanged. `string` and `string?` are both exactly System.String at the IL/runtime level. (b) Nullable<T> is only for value types, this doesn't apply to reference types. (c) no runtime checks are inserted. (d) string remains a reference type either way.

questions.question: A `required` property is left unset in an object initializer. When does this get caught?

choices.text: At runtime, the first time the property is read
At runtime, when the object is garbage collected
It's never caught — required is documentation only
At compile time — the compiler reports an error

questions.explanation: required is enforced entirely at compile time as part of object-initializer resolution: any construction site that omits a required member is a compile error, not a runtime issue. (a) and (b) both incorrectly place the check at runtime. (c) required has real compiler enforcement, it's not just documentation.

questions.question: A primary constructor parameter is only used to initialize a readonly property and never referenced elsewhere in the type. Does the compiler still generate hidden field storage for that parameter?

choices.text: Yes, always, regardless of how the parameter is used
No — storage is only generated when actually needed
Only for record types, never for plain classes or structs
Only if the parameter type is a reference type

questions.explanation: The compiler only creates hidden storage for a primary constructor parameter if it's referenced somewhere in a member of the type after construction. If it's only used to initialize a property/field once, no extra field is generated for the parameter itself. (a) overstates it — storage isn't unconditional. (c) this behavior applies to plain classes/structs too, not just records. (d) the parameter's type doesn't determine whether storage is generated.
